title: financiers are set turn nvidia into an ai baron 2026 09 02
author: Karen Kwok
text:
NEW YORK, Sept 2 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Nvidia (NVDA.O)
, opens new tab
 and artificial intelligence are practically synonymous: wherever a new chatbot-powering data center springs up, the chipmaker’s silicon is usually found. Making up 60% of the cost of an AI-focused server farm, according to boss Jensen Huang
, opens new tab
, these processors are a huge part of the trillions of dollars being spent on infrastructure. Marshalling the resources necessary to finance this expenditure requires certainty. So ​too do the labs spending billions each year to rent the resulting computing power. A nascent market for futures contracts is a way to provide it – and cement Nvidia’s products as the de facto ‌oil barrels of the AI era.
Frequently shorthanded as “compute,” a mélange of GPUs, CPUs, networking gear and server racks is essential to enable chatbots to train on reams of data and process user queries. These resources are both scarce and inefficiently distributed. Data-center vacancy rates in North America sit at around
, opens new tab
 1%, while roughly 92% of new capacity is already pre-committed before construction, according to Boston Consulting Group. Yet a gigantic, 500,000-strong cluster of Nvidia GPUs operated by Elon Musk’s xAI was running at utilization rates of only about 11% in April, The Information reported
, opens new tab
.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, the price to rent ​a GPU is therefore volatile and inconsistent. According to figures gathered by Silicon Data, an hour of time on one of Nvidia’s H100 chips operated by a so-called hyperscaler like Microsoft (MSFT.O)
, opens new tab
 or Amazon.com (AMZN.O)
, opens new tab
 costs $7.23. On smaller cloud providers, ​that drops to $2.65.
In a way, it’s reminiscent of early markets for other commodities. Rudimentary futures contracts – a promise to deliver, say, grain at a given time and at a pre-determined ⁠price – helped smooth out seasonal booms and shortages in the nineteenth century. Eventually, as economic output became critically dependent on the supply of fossil-fuel energy, oil futures aided in taming the volatile market of the 1980s. Importantly, contracts like the West ​Texas Intermediate, or WTI, futures set a global benchmark price.
Now, a growing chunk of the economy is set to depend on the supply of computing power. The comparison might not be so ridiculous. At roughly 105 million barrels a day, as estimated ​by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the global oil market would represent around $2.7 trillion of annual physical consumption at $70 a barrel. BCG estimates
, opens new tab
 that the AI compute market could reach up to $2.4 trillion by 2030.
Indeed, Wall Street is already springing into action. CME Group (CME.O)
, opens new tab
 plans to launch compute futures this month, linked to Silicon Data’s indices. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE.N)
, opens new tab
 is planning its own version, using data from Ornn.
Much as oil drillers want more clarity on returns from their big up-front investments in opening a new spigot, data-center builders could benefit from hedging against future price drops. And just ​as an airline wants to be able to protect against rising costs to fuel its planes, Anthropic could use a way to guard against sudden spikes in rental prices. Given that the Claude maker is paying the equivalent of $50 billion per gigawatt ​of computing capacity to xAI, compared to much lower implied rates charged by server farm operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O)
, opens new tab
, a transparent benchmark could also help when negotiating oddball bilateral deals.
One complication is that, unlike grain or oil futures that involve delivering the underlying product, an hour of GPU ‌usage cannot ⁠be held in storage somewhere. ICE’s planned futures
, opens new tab
 are instead cash-settled, meaning that money simply changes hands at the end of the contract, rather than the good itself.
Furthermore, no two chips are quite alike. AMD (AMD.O)
, opens new tab
 also makes GPUs. Intel (INTC.O)
, opens new tab
 and ARM design CPUs. Alphabet (GOOGL.O)
, opens new tab
, OpenAI, Amazon and Microsoft are all lighting up their own specialized, in-house silicon. Nvidia, though, is easily the industry benchmark, with an estimated
, opens new tab
 market share of over 80%. A custom chip used by one or two customers may be technically powerful, but holds little value for a broad market of buyers who would need to rejig their systems to use it. The H100, by contrast, is practically plug-and-play.
Little wonder, then, that CME and ICE’s contracts are tied to rental prices for Nvidia’s chips, for now. That’s ​a coup for Huang, who has pushed to remain the ​de facto industry standard. Those efforts span everything from ⁠investing in upstart cloud providers, helping to ensure there are plenty of operators supplying its wares to the market, all the way to a $500 billion plan to provide customer financing from private lenders like Apollo Global Management (APO.N)
, opens new tab
 and Blackstone (BX.N)
, opens new tab
.
Becoming the anchor for benchmark compute prices can further that plan. Sure, big technology companies like Microsoft can fund AI infrastructure with cash flow or ​unsecured debt. But AI labs like Anthropic or smaller cloud operators like CoreWeave, without the benefit of stellar credit ratings, need help. Lenders have already agreed to some loans ​backed by GPUs, and Nvidia’s silicon ⁠is the most dependable collateral around. Yet making this common practice without the lure of a contract to serve a blue-chip customer like Meta Platforms (META.O)
, opens new tab
 is tricky. A particular issue is that the long-term value of an H100, when Huang’s company regularly releases new and speedier chips, is uncertain.
Futures are a neat way for lenders to hedge against that risk. Assuming there’s $3.6 trillion of AI infrastructure investment from 2026 through 2030, BCG analysts estimate that a reliable forward curve of compute prices could help reduce borrowing costs by about $116 ⁠billion in total, or ​roughly $26 billion a year.
Of course, as Alphabet or Amazon try to broaden adoption of their own chips, competing futures could badly fragment the market. ​Moreover, an H100 hour in Texas is not necessarily equivalent to – or as valuable as – one in Virginia or Europe. Big, bilateral contracts struck at ad hoc terms might render spot prices of surplus capacity less meaningful. And, most importantly of all, this all redounds largely to the benefit of Nvidia specifically. ​That’s unlike oil, where barrels of the same grade are essentially equivalent, whether provided by Chevron or Exxon. If compute is the new crude, Huang is a baron like no other.
